card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility trade-off inherent to traditional alloys be overcome in multi-principal-element alloys by exploiting multiple levels of heterogeneities?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) including FCC-based systems (e.g., CoCrFeNi, CrCoNi, VCoNi), BCC-based refractory systems (e.g., TiZrHfNbTa), dual-phase eutectic lamella HEAs, and alloys with multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles (MCINPs). Processing: Partial recrystallization to create heterogeneous grain structures (HGS), spinodal decomposition to form precipitates, addition of oxygen solutes (~2 at%) to form nanoscale complexes, and intentional alloying to tune stacking fault energy (SFE) for deformation-induced transformations. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) uniaxial tensile testing; cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K) for specific FCC MEAs; compression testing for some refractory BCC HEAs. Findings: An FCC-MCINP alloy achieved a yield strength above 1 GPa with a uniform elongation (εu) of ~50%, showing no strength–ductility trade-off compared to unstrengthened elemental metals.; A single-phase CrCoNi MEA with a heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nano-to-micro scales reached a gigapascal yield strength while maintaining εu in excess of 20%.; The VCoNi MEA achieved near-GPa yield strength with εu ~30% and total elongation ~38%, attributed to maximized lattice friction from atomic size mismatch.; In BCC-TiZrHfNb HEA, adding ~2 at% oxygen formed nanoscale (O, Ti, Zr)-complexes that increased tensile elongation from ~14% to ~28% while maintaining high strength.; Stress-assisted martensitic transformation in BCC-Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 HEA created a 65% volume fraction of internally twinned martensite, doubling the strain-hardening rate.; Wide hysteresis loops in load–unload–reload stress–strain curves demonstrated that nonhomogeneous plastic deformation in HGS alloys imparts high back stresses contributing to strain hardening.; At cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K), the CrCoNi MEA exhibited strain-hardening rates and εu comparable to the best 316 austenitic stainless steels due to reduced dynamic recovery.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high concentration of multiple principal elements creates a rugged energy landscape with statistical fluctuations in composition and local chemical order (LCO), causing dislocations to adopt a wavy line and face intermittent 'nanoscale segment detrapping' barriers. This intrinsic lattice friction is compounded by a hierarchy of heterogeneities (defects, precipitates, grain boundaries, phase boundaries) that promote nonhomogeneous plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocation storage, and dynamic mechanisms like twinning (TWIP) and transformation (TRIP), which sustain high strain-hardening rates to delay necking.. Limitations: Refractory BCC HEAs often lack room-temperature tensile ductility due to a drastic rise in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature; TRIP-assisted DP alloys with low initial yield strength require hardening (e.g., cold work) which causes the strain-hardening rate to become inadequate, restoring the strength–ductility trade-off at high σy levels.. Future work: Continued endeavors to tailor heterogeneities to ward off plastic instabilities and realize even better strength–ductility balance, expanding the repertoire of alloys in compositions and properties through refined and enhanced HEAs.. Quote: "The strength of HEAs is considerably higher than traditional solid solutions, as the many constituents lead to a rugged energy landscape that increases the resistance to dislocation motion."

W2554394793.title: Directly cast bulk eutectic and near-eutectic high entropy alloys with balanced strength and ductility in a wide temperature range

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys be improved by inheriting the composite lamellar nature through tailored thermo-mechanical processing?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Arc-melting followed by suction-casting into a copper mold, multi-pass cold-rolling to 84–86% reduction in thickness, and non-isothermal annealing at 660, 700, 740, or 900 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests with an initial strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4 s−1 using dog-bone specimens (15 mm gauge length, 3.2 mm width, 600 μm thickness) and loading–unloading–reloading (LUR) tests.. Findings: The DPHL700 and DPHL740 samples achieved a yield strength of approximately 1.5 GPa with an elongation of ~16%, representing a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to as-cast and ultrafine-grained counterparts.; The microstructure exhibited a two-hierarchical heterogeneity consisting of submicron-grade FCC/B2 grains within FCC lamellae and micron-grade alternate FCC/B2 lamellae.; The average diameters of FCC and B2 grains were roughly comparable at ~0.71 μm, with inter-lamella spacings ranging from 1.5 to 5 μm.; Phase decomposition resulted in two types of NiAl-rich precipitates in FCC lamellae: small intragranular P1 grains (50–180 nm) and large intergranular P2 grains (~350 nm).; Back-stress measurements at the yield point reached ~950 MPa, which was approximately 3 times higher than the effective stress, primarily responsible for the high yield strength.; The strain-hardening rate (Θ) showed a transient behavior with an up-turn in region II and sustained high Θ over a wide strain region III for DPHL700.; Microcrack-arresting mechanisms were observed where multiple microcracks were inhibited from coalescing, with ductile components acting as efficient crack arresters.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced properties to a two-hierarchical constraint effect that generates long-range back-stress by storing geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) due to strain gradients at lamella interfaces and around intergranular precipitates, combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism where the aligned lamellar architecture delays crack propagation and coalescence.. Limitations: The authors note that while the DPHL structure is effective, increasing the annealing temperature to 900 °C induced a partially degraded lamellar structure that led to inferior tensile properties, indicating the sensitivity of the process to thermal treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that further efforts should be devoted to exploring non-equiatomic alloys and spinodal decomposition to create low-misfit coherent nanostructures for even higher yield strengths, and anticipate modifying the EHEA to satisfy requirements for high-temperature and/or corrosion environments.. Quote: "The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism."

card: Paper card. Question: How can room-temperature deformation twinning be induced in a high-entropy alloy to improve cryogenic tensile properties, and can non-recrystallized grains be utilized to achieve ultra-high yield strength while maintaining ductility?. System: 10V15Cr5Mn35Fe10Co25Ni (at.%) high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization at 1,100 °C for 6 h; cold rolling at room temperature with a 75% reduction ratio to produce 1.5-mm-thick sheets; annealing at 750 °C for 10 min to obtain partially recrystallized microstructure (H750) or at 900 °C for 10 min for fully recrystallized microstructure (H900); water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature and cryogenic temperature (−196 °C) using a crosshead speed of 6.4 × 10−3 mm s−1.. Findings: The H750 alloy achieved a yield strength of 970 MPa and a tensile strength of 1,314 MPa at cryogenic temperatures.; The H750 alloy maintained a persistent elongation of 46.3% at cryogenic temperatures.; Non-recrystallized grains in the H750 alloy had an average size of ~32 μm, while recrystallized grains averaged ~1.5 μm.; Deformation twins with thicknesses of 10–30 nm were observed in recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.; Primary twin bundles of ~500 nm thickness and secondary twins of 30–70 nm thickness formed in non-recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.; The yield strength of the H750 alloy was ~270 MPa higher than that of the fully recrystallized H900 alloy at cryogenic temperatures.; Room-temperature cold rolling induced deformation twins in coarse grains without prior hot rolling, which were retained after partial recrystallization.. Mechanism: The critical stress for twinning decreases with increasing grain size, allowing twins to form readily in coarse non-recrystallized grains during cold rolling at room temperature. These retained twins act as strong barriers against mobile dislocations, enhancing yield strength. At cryogenic temperatures, additional deformation twins form in both recrystallized and non-recrystallized regions, leading to a high strain-hardening effect and ultra-high strength.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that non-recrystallized regions are generally avoided in conventional alloys due to deleterious effects on ductility.. Future work: The authors propose that the combination of room-temperature deformation twinning and non-recrystallization offers a strengthening mechanism for ultra-high-strength HEAs and suggest the alloy is promising for applications in ultra-high-strength HEAs at cryogenic temperatures.. Quote: "Our results demonstrate that non-recrystallized grains, which are generally avoided in conventional alloys because of their deleterious effect on ductility, can be useful in achieving high-strength high-entropy alloys."

Question: How can the stability of austenite in Fe-Mn-Al duplex lightweight steels be optimized to achieve a combination of high tensile strength and high ductility without the steady flow behavior (plastic instability) observed in previous (TRIP+TWIP) steels?. System: Fe-0.3C-9Mn-5Al (modified) and Fe-0.3C-8.5Mn-5.6Al (previous) duplex lightweight steels; annealed variants A850, A900, A950. Processing: Vacuum induction melting; homogenization at 1200 °C for 1 hour; hot-rolling between 1100 °C and 900 °C; furnace cooling from 650 °C; cold rolling to 1 mm; annealing at 850, 900, or 950 °C for 5 min; cooling to 400 °C at -14 °C s⁻¹ followed by air cooling. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ using ASTM E 8/E 8 M standard specimens (gage length 25 mm, width 6 mm, thickness 1 mm). Findings: The modified Fe-0.3C-9Mn-5Al steel annealed at 900 °C (A900) achieved a tensile strength of 874 MPa and elongation of 72%.; The A850 steel (annealed at 850 °C) exhibited an elongation of 95% with a tensile strength of 785 MPa.; The A900 steel showed the highest true tensile strength of 1496 MPa among the annealed variants.; The A950 steel (annealed at 950 °C) showed an abrupt reduction in elongation to about 25% despite a tensile strength of 840 MPa.; In the A900 steel, the volume fraction of martensite increased by 30% from Stage B to failure, compared to 15% in the A850 steel.; Plastic instability did not occur in the A900 steel until failure because the strain hardening rate remained considerably higher than the true stress.; The austenite fraction in the modified steel was 56% after 66%-cold-rolling and annealing at 900 °C for 30 min.; The austenite grain size in the A900 steel was 2.1 μm, compared to 1.7 μm in A850 and 2.6 μm in A950.. Mechanism: The authors argue that decreasing austenite stability (indirectly via increased austenite fraction and alloying partitioning) promotes a dominant TRIP mechanism over TWIP in the A900 steel. This active TRIP, occurring at lower critical strains with higher rates, generates a high strain hardening rate that delays plastic instability. In contrast, the A850 steel retains high stability leading to simultaneous TRIP and TWIP, which maximizes ductility (95%) but results in steady flow behavior (plastic instability) after initial hardening. The A950 steel has too low stability, causing rapid transformation and early failure.. Limitations: The authors state that the A850 steel, despite its 95% elongation, still exhibits steady flow behavior (plastic instability) which is a drawback for structural applications requiring high strain hardening. Additionally, the A950 steel suffers from seriously reduced elongation due to a transformation rate that is too high.. Future work: The authors propose that the A900 steel, with its outstanding tensile properties and reduced density, gives a promise for automotive applications as highly-deformable high-strength sheets and structural reinforcement components requiring high stiffness.. Quote: "The present work gives a promise for structural applications requiring both reduced specific weight and remarkable deformability."

card: Paper card. Question: Whether it is necessary to use all five elements (Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr) to achieve a random solid solution and good mechanical properties, or if reducing the system to 3 or 4 elements yields similar results.. System: HfNbTaTiZr system; specific alloys: HfNbTaTiZr (5-element), NbTaTiZr, NbTaTi, NbTiZr, TaTiZr, Nb0.5TaTiZr1.5, Nb1.5TaTiZr0.5 (3 and 4-element MEAs).. Processing: Vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible; elements with 99.9% purity; ingots cast 8 times and flipped for mixing; no Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) or heat treatment applied to cast material.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1; Vickers hardness HV30 measurements; microstructure and phase analysis via SEM, WDS, and XRD.. Findings: The 5-element HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation among all studied alloys.; The 4-element NbTaTiZr alloy has similar strength to the 5-element alloy but reduced elongation to 6.4%.; The TaTiZr alloy exhibited brittle behavior, breaking before reaching the yield point.; The NbTaTi alloy showed the highest elongation and the lowest hardness of 246 HV.; Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr resulted in a significant reduction of ductility due to a reduction in BCC1 phase content.; Precipitation of Ta-rich particles on grain boundaries reduced maximum elongation to failure to zero values in brittle alloys.; A clear linear relationship exists between total elongation and the BCC1 phase content.; Grain size was estimated around 0.5 mm for all alloys except NbTiZr, which showed no dendritic segregation.. Mechanism: The simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr causes segregation during solidification due to a miscibility gap in the Ta-Zr binary phase diagram, leading to the formation of two BCC phases (BCC1 and BCC2) and intergranular Ta-rich precipitates. The reduction in the BCC1 phase content and the presence of these precipitates on grain boundaries are responsible for the significant reduction in ductility and the transition to brittle fracture.. Limitations: The study did not investigate the BCC2 and BCC3 phases or intergranular precipitates in detail. The relation between hardness and the misfit parameter δ is complicated because not all alloys are single-phase. The role of rapid cooling versus chemical composition in phase stability requires further verification.. Future work: Further research shall focus on detailed investigations of the BCC2 and BCC3 phases and intergranular precipitates. The destabilizing effect of Ta + Zr on BCC phase stability during manufacturing and aging shall be verified. The stabilizing effect of Hf on HCP phase formation during mid-temperature aging and the influence of cooling rate on phase composition shall be investigated.. Quote: "Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content."

card: Paper card. Question: Does a single-phase high entropy alloy exhibit inverse Hall-Petch behavior and low friction/wear in an ultra-high vacuum environment, and what is the underlying mechanism?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (FCC single-phase). Processing: Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS) additive manufacturing using 45–75 µm gas atomized powder; laser power 350–400 W, build velocity 400–600 mm/min, layer thickness 250–300 µm, hatch spacing 800 µm, in <50 ppm O2 atmosphere; initial average grain size ~42 µm. Test conditions: Ultra-high vacuum (~10⁻⁹ torr), room temperature, rotary sliding with 3.2 mm sapphire sphere, loads of 10 mN and 100 mN, angular velocity ~15.5 rpm, stroke length 45°, up to 20k cycles. Findings: Steady-state friction coefficients of μss ≅ 0.32 at 10 mN and μss ≅ 0.68 at 100 mN were measured in UHV.; Specific wear rates were remarkably low at ~10⁻⁶ mm³/N-m for the initially soft, coarse-grained material.; STEM validation showed dynamic grain refinement to an average size of d = 13 ± 5 nm (upper bound) or 2–3 nm during sliding, with amorphous regions present.; A pause in sliding for 24 hours caused the friction coefficient to increase to μ ≅ 0.55, implying grain growth to ~5 nm.; The dynamic amorphization model predicted an average high angle grain boundary energy of 0.87 J/m².; Cavitation-induced nanoporosity was observed in the highly deformed surface layer, linked to the predicted high grain boundary energy.. Mechanism: The authors attribute low friction and wear to shear-induced dynamic amorphization and extreme grain refinement below a critical size (dcrit ≅ 10–50 nm), where grain boundary sliding becomes energetically favorable over dislocation activity, leading to inverse Hall-Petch behavior and a near-amorphous surface layer.. Limitations: Ex situ techniques like TEM and nanoindentation are not ideal for determining the actual grain size during sliding because the ultra-nanocrystalline surface layers are extremely thin and prone to rapid grain growth and recrystallization after the test.. Future work: The authors suggest that the observed phenomena may indicate low temperature and high strain rate superplasticity, implying a need to further explore the link between grain boundary decohesion, cavitation, and superplasticity in HEAs.. Quote: "Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m)"

card: Paper card. Question: What is the fundamental mechanism responsible for the loss of ductility with increasing temperature in single-phase face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys, specifically CrMnFeCoNi?. System: Equiatomic Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 (single-phase) and nonequiatomic Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 (dual-phase with Cr-rich σ). Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere, homogenization at 1200°C for 48 hours, hot rolling at 1100°C to 8 mm, cold rolling to 2.4 mm (70% reduction), annealing at 1000°C for 1 hour (single-phase) or 900°C for 1 hour (dual-phase). Test conditions: Quasi-static tensile tests at 25° to 800°C, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹, samples held at temperature for ~10 min before testing. Findings: Ductility loss in single-phase Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 occurs at intermediate temperatures (400° to 700°C) with fracture shortly after ultimate tensile stress.; Fracture mode changes from fully ductile transgranular failure at 25°C to mixed brittle intergranular and ductile transgranular failure at 700°C.; Atom probe tomography reveals nanosized regions (~5 nm thickness) at grain boundaries enriched with Cr, Ni, and Mn after testing at 700°C.; No second-phase precipitates were detected along grain boundaries by XRD, TEM, or SEM-EDS after testing at 700°C.; Cr and Ni segregate separately at grain boundaries, while Ni and Mn tend to cosegregate.; The dual-phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 alloy exhibits increased ductility with temperature and no intergranular embrittlement at 600° and 700°C.; Trace elements C and B segregate at grain boundaries but at concentrations (0.2 at% C, 0.008 at% B) insufficient to form carbides or borides.. Mechanism: Ductility loss is caused by the fast segregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) into grain boundaries during deformation at intermediate temperatures, forming nanoclusters that reduce grain boundary cohesion and promote crack initiation. The authors propose that Cr and Ni segregate separately due to repulsion, while Ni and Mn cosegregate, potentially forming brittle phases or reducing cohesion via magnetic contributions. Preexisting Cr-rich σ phases can absorb these embrittling elements, preventing their segregation to grain boundaries.. Limitations: The study notes that grain refinement in HEAs can assist the segregation of principal elements to grain boundaries and lead to brittle intermetallic phases, making grain refinement ineffective for avoiding this specific embrittlement. Additionally, the dual-phase alloy designed for proof-of-concept has lower ductility than the single-phase alloy below 500°C.. Future work: The authors suggest that the ductility of HEAs at intermediate temperatures can be further improved if the morphology, dimension, and distribution of secondary phases are optimized further following the proposed GB segregation engineering strategy.. Quote: "Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs."

card: Paper card. Question: Does the mere increase in the number of constituent elements in high entropy alloys (HEAs) lead to sluggish grain boundary diffusion, and how does the nature of added constituents affect diffusion kinetics compared to pure metals and binary alloys?. System: CoCrFeNi (quaternary) and CoCrFeMnNi (quinary) high entropy alloys with equiatomic proportions. Processing: Arc melting of 99.99 wt.% purity solid pieces in equiatomic proportions, re-melted 4–5 times for homogeneity, followed by homogenization at 1473 K for 50 h; samples cut to 8 mm diameter and 1 mm thickness, mechanically polished, and subjected to diffusion annealing at 673 K, 723 K, 873 K, 1073 K, and 1173 K. Test conditions: Radiotracer analysis using 63Ni isotope (68 keV β-decays) deposited on sample surfaces; annealing in quartz tubes under 5 N purified Ar atmosphere; serial sectioning with 0.3 μm thickness for low-temperature measurements; grain size >250 μm; absence of elemental segregation confirmed by Atom Probe Tomography (APT) at 60 K. Findings: Grain boundary width (δ) estimated at approximately 0.5 nm for both alloys, consistent with FCC metals.; Grain boundary energies estimated at 0.8–0.9 J/m² and found to increase significantly with temperature, more pronounced in CoCrFeMnNi.; Ni GB diffusion in CoCrFeMnNi is slower than in CoCrFeNi below 800 K, but the trend reverses at higher temperatures.; Ni GB diffusion in CoCrFeNi is slower by only an order of magnitude compared to pure Ni and binary Fe-Ni alloys.; CoCrFeMnNi exhibits the largest activation energy for both GB and bulk tracer diffusion of Ni among the studied systems.; A cross-over temperature (Tc) of 800 K exists for GB diffusion, below which CoCrFeMnNi is slower and above which it is faster than CoCrFeNi.; The segregation factor (s) for Ni at grain boundaries is approximately unity, confirmed by APT showing no elemental segregation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the cross-over behavior and diffusion rates to two opposing effects of Mn addition: (i) an increase in the average negative enthalpy of mixing (from -3 kJ/mol in CoCrFeNi to -4.25 kJ/mol in CoCrFeMnNi) which increases energy barriers, and (ii) a decrease in the melting temperature of the alloy. They argue that the chemically disordered matrix increases energy barriers in CoCrFeMnNi, while reduced diffusion entropy contributions affect CoCrFeNi, concluding that decreased diffusion is not solely a function of configurational entropy.. Limitations: The study notes that a systematic investigation on fully characterized bicrystals is required to explain the intriguing behavior of GB energy decreasing with temperature in pure materials versus increasing in alloys, and that the exact value of GB energy is important for phase stability but requires further study.. Future work: The authors state that a detailed investigation of the structure and properties of grain boundaries in these HEAs would be required to explain the observed temperature coefficients of GB energy, which is beyond the scope of the present study.. Quote: "Our GB diffusion measurements prove that a mere increase in number of constituent elements does not lower the diffusion rates in HEAs, but the nature of added constituents plays a more decisive role."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the compiled mechanical properties of high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) be used to assess their potential as structural materials and guide future development?. System: 370 high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), including 3d transition metal, refractory metal (RHEAs and RCCAs), light metal family, and bronzes and brasses HEAs/CCAs families; HEAs defined as alloys with 5 or more principal elements (5-35 at%); CCAs defined as alloys with 3 or more principal components.. Processing: Compilation of data from published reports from 2004 to 2016; density estimated using rule of mixtures (ROM): ρ=∑xiMi/∑xiVi; Young's modulus estimated using ROM for single phase solid solutions only: E=∑xiEi.. Test conditions: Uniaxial loading (tension or compression) at room temperature for 370 alloys; temperature-dependent testing for 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs).. Findings: The database covers mechanical properties for 370 HEAs and CCAs reported between 2004 and 2016.; For 27 refractory HEAs, yield stress and elongation are provided as a function of testing temperature.; The database includes alloy composition, microstructure type, density, hardness, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength, and Young's modulus.; Data entries are organized in a tree-like classification with four families and expanded into classes based on principal element combinations.; The database enables users to browse, search, filter, and plot material property maps using performance indices defined by M. F. Ashby.. Mechanism: The authors explain that HEAs are presumably stabilized by the configurational entropy of mixing, while CCAs encompass a broader range of alloys with single-phase or multi-phase microstructures; the database allows for the evaluation of performance indices for lighter, stronger, and stiffer structures.. Limitations: The properties are not equally populated for every alloy due to the lack of literature data.. Future work: The database can be used to represent various property spaces, calculate performance indices, and enable data mining to extract insights and uncover patterns to guide and accelerate the development of HEAs and CCAs.. Quote: "The database covers the main mechanical properties of HEAs and CCAs tested under uniaxial loading from published reports since 2004 until end of 2016."

card: Paper card. Question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via in-situ alloy formation using laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence defect formation, microstructure, and phase composition?. System: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 (refractory metal high entropy alloy) fabricated from a heterogeneous mixture of elemental W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V powders.. Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm) on a Mo substrate in Argon atmosphere (<25 ppm O2). Two parameter sets were used: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch, 125 J/mm³) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch, 889 J/mm³). Vanadium powder content was increased by a factor of 1.5 to compensate for evaporation.. Test conditions: Samples (6 × 6 × 6 mm³) were analyzed via optical microscopy, SEM, EBSD, TEM, and microhardness testing. Microhardness was measured as HV0.1. Cooling rates are estimated at 10⁶ K/s.. Findings: Relative densities reached 99.8% for parameter set A and 99.5% for parameter set B.; A single bcc-phase was confirmed by EBSD and TEM, consistent with vacuum arc melted samples.; Average grain size was 16.3 µm for PBF-LB/M B, which is more than four times smaller than the 80 µm reported for vacuum arc melted samples.; Parameter set B (higher volumetric energy density) resulted in fewer undissolved tungsten particles compared to set A.; Parameter set A exhibited smaller cracks than set B, which showed wider cracks due to higher internal stress.; Microhardness of the coarser structure (Set A) was 561 ± 17 HV0.1, while the finer cellular structure (Set B) was 614 ± 21 HV0.1.; Elemental segregation was observed: V concentrated in interdendritic areas, while W and Ta were predominantly in intradendritic areas.; Solidification mode shifted from dendritic (Set A) to cellular (Set B) based on growth rate (R) and temperature gradient (G) conditions.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the formation of undissolved W particles to the high melting point of tungsten, which requires high volumetric energy input and slow scan speeds to dissolve. Cracking is caused by internal stresses from the PBF-LB/M process combined with the alloy's low room temperature ductility and brittle grain boundaries (likely due to O and N impurities). The microstructure (dendritic vs. cellular) is controlled by the ratio of growth rate (R) to temperature gradient (G), where higher R and lower G favor dendrites, while lower R and higher G favor cellular structures.. Limitations: Samples contained cracks and undissolved tungsten particles; completely defect-free samples were not produced. The study notes that the alloy has limited room temperature ductility and fracture toughness.. Future work: The authors suggest using a high-temperature (>600 °C) build-platform heating device and/or high-purity powder with low O and N content to achieve crack-free processing. They also propose verifying if more recently developed refractory metal high entropy alloys with increased room temperature ductility can be processed without high-temperature heating.. Quote: "The relative density of the samples with a dimension of 6 × 6 × 6 mm3 reaches, in dependence of the PBF-LB/M parameter set, 99.8%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (Refractory High Entropy Alloy). Processing: 1. Vacuum/argon arc melting followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under 210 MPa argon. 2. Homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 hours followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature (Condition 1). 3. Solutionizing Condition 1 at 1400 °C for 20 min followed by water quenching (Condition 2). 4. Annealing Condition 2 at 600 °C for 120 hrs followed by water quenching (Condition 3).. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) and 600 °C uniaxial compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001 s−1; Vickers microhardness (4.9 N load, 15 s dwell); Microstructural characterization via SEM, TEM, and Atom Probe Tomography (APT).. Findings: Condition (1) (continuous B2 matrix) exhibited a yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compressive strain before fracture.; Condition (2) (single-phase weakly ordered BCC) showed high ductility with no fracture after 60% true strain but lower yield strength (1065 MPa).; Condition (3) (inverted microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates in continuous BCC matrix) achieved a yield strength of 1345 MPa and 16.9% peak strain with fracture at 38% strain.; At 600 °C, Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than its RT value of 1345 MPa) and 16.2% plasticity.; APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phase is rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phase is rich in Nb and Ta.; The microstructure of Condition (3) consists of discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) within a continuous disordered BCC matrix, contrasting with Condition (1) where B2 is the continuous matrix.; Condition (1) hardness was 562 ± 16 HV, Condition (2) was 405 ± 11 HV, and Condition (3) was 475 ± 12 HV.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the poor ductility in Condition (1) is caused by the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is attributed to the 'inversion' of the microstructure, where the continuous phase becomes the more ductile disordered BCC matrix, while the hard B2 phase exists as discrete precipitates providing strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, similar to mechanisms in Ni3Al.. Limitations: The authors state that the details of the strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study and that the explanation for the anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative. They note that applying classical precipitation hardening models requires parameters (lattice misfit, elastic properties, fault energies) that are difficult to quantify in this complex RHEA.. Future work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and additional studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.. card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying tungsten concentration affect the crystal structure, microstructure, and mechanical properties (hardness, strength, ductility) of WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys fabricated via laser cladding deposition?. System: WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys with x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53 (mole fractions). Processing: Laser cladding deposition (LCD) using a coaxial LCD system with 565 W laser power, 8 mm/s scanning speed, 0.08 mm layer thickness, and 600 °C induction heating temperature; powders (45–125 μm) mixed for 4 h and dried at 120 °C for 8 h in Argon (<80 ppm O2). Test conditions: Vickers microhardness (500 g load, 30 s); room temperature compression (25 °C, 0.001 s⁻¹); high-temperature compression (1000 °C, 3.5 min heating, 15 min soak, 0.001 s⁻¹ strain rate, 10⁻³ torr vacuum). Findings: All WxNbMoTa alloys formed a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution regardless of tungsten content.; Grain and dendrite sizes averaged 20 μm and 4 μm, respectively, due to rapid solidification in LCD.; Vickers microhardness increased with tungsten concentration: 459.2 ± 9.7, 476.0 ± 12.9, 485.3 ± 8.7, and 497.6 ± 5.6 Hv for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; NbMoTa (x = 0) exhibited yield strength of 530 MPa and compressive strain of 8.5% at 1000 °C.; At room temperature, NbMoTa showed yield strength of 874 MPa and compressive strain of 5.8%, while W-containing alloys were brittle with compressive strengths of 840–895 MPa.; Bulk modulus increased with tungsten content: 174, 182, 186, and 192 GPa for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; Spherical gas porosities in as-fabricated samples were eliminated by using molybdenum powders with higher granule density and good sphericity.. Mechanism: Rapid solidification during laser cladding deposition (melting in 10⁻³–10⁻² s) suppresses constitutional segregation and promotes fine equiaxed grains. Tungsten addition increases lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening, raising hardness and bulk modulus but reducing ductility at room temperature. Porosity formation is attributed to adsorbed Argon gas in low-density molybdenum powder particles, not microstructure features.. Limitations: Spherical gas porosities appeared in samples fabricated with standard molybdenum powders due to low granule density; tungsten addition reduces room-temperature plasticity, making W-containing alloys brittle.. Future work: The present work provides a theoretical basis for LCD manufacturing of aerospace parts of refractory HEAs with large size, complex structure, and variable composition.. Quote: "The size of the grains and dendrites are 20 μm and 4 μm on average, due to the rapid solidification characteristics of the laser cladding deposition."

card: Paper card. Question: Can independently controllable multiple coherent precipitation structures be tailored by stepwise thermo-mechanical processes to generate ultrahigh strength and ductile refractory high-entropy alloys?. System: (W1.5Ni2.25Fe)95Ta5 (at.%) refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting of pure metals, homogenization at 1200 °C for 5 h, hot-rolling at 1200 °C (80% reduction), cold-rolling at 25 °C (75% reduction), annealing at 900 °C for 5 min, and aging at 650 °C for 20 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature (strain rate 5 × 10−4 s−1) and elevated temperatures up to 800 °C (strain rate 10−3 s−1). Findings: The alloy achieved an ultrahigh ultimate tensile strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature.; The yield strength of the as-cast structure was ~600 MPa, increasing to ~1.4 GPa after Step I (δ-lamella precipitation) and further to 2.0 GPa after Step II (γ″-particle precipitation).; The alloy retained a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C.; The δ-lamellar precipitates have a width of ~40 nm and a length ranging from 0.5 to 1 μm.; The γ″ precipitates are spheroidal with a size of ~10 nm.; Both the δ and γ″ precipitates were identified with the composition (Ni70Fe5)3(Ta20W5).; The lattice misfit between the γ″ precipitates and the matrix was measured to be ~0.013.; The microstructure remained stable after annealing at 800 °C for 50 h (δ phase) and 40 h (γ″ phase).. Mechanism: The coherent interfaces of the stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations; dislocations shear the δ-lamellae leading to coherent misalignment rather than crack formation, while the small size and low lattice misfit of γ″ particles prevent crack initiation at the precipitate-matrix interface, collectively enabling high strength and ductility.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design.. Findings: Achieved ultimate tensile strength (σu) of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation (εue) of 13% in the CRAA-treated alloy.; The dual heterogeneous structure consists of a matrix with coarse grains (10–30 μm) and ultra-fine grains (0.5–2 μm).; Heterogeneous L12 nanoprecipitates range from several to hundreds of nanometers with a total volume fraction of 24.2%.; The lattice mismatch between the FCC matrix and L12 precipitates is extremely low at 0.011%.; The average size of fine L12 precipitates is 4.14 ± 0.62 nm with a number density of 3.4 × 1024 m−3.; Strengthening contributions calculated as: solid-solution (49 MPa), HDI hardening (800 MPa), and precipitation hardening (1115 MPa).; No twins or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase formed after deformation up to ~2.0 GPa stress.; Dislocation density in the fractured sample reached 3.83 × 1014 m−2 due to Lomer–Cottrell locks.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior properties to a combination of HDI strengthening from the heterogeneous grain structure, precipitation hardening from high-density coherent L12 particles, and enhanced ductility from the low elastic misfit strain of the interfaces which relieves stress concentration and prevents premature fracture, while the preservation of stacking faults and high dislocation density provides significant work-hardening.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors state that the strategy opens a new avenue for the development of promising heavy-duty structural materials and that the alloy elements and treatments can be readily accepted by industry.. Quote: "a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a dual heterogeneous structure of both matrix and precipitates can be designed to provide an ultra-high tensile strength of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation of 13%"

card: Paper card. Question: Can a hierarchical architecture involving secondary nanoprecipitates form inside primary nanoprecipitates in high-entropy alloys, and can an ultrahigh strength be achieved through a high density of such intragranular hierarchical nanoprecipitates?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (atomic %). Processing: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 49 hours (45h dry + 4h wet with ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1000°C, 30 MPa pressure, 90°C/min heating rate, and <8 Pa vacuum.. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension using in situ SEM microtensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM compression tests at room temperature with an axial displacement rate of 3 nm s–1.. Findings: Tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.; Failure strain of ~5.2% achieved alongside the ultrahigh strength values.; Microstructure consists of a primary fcc phase (~82.3 vol %) and a small amount of bcc phase (~17.7 vol %).; The fcc matrix contains a high density of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates: primary γ′ (L12 structure, ~57 nm avg diameter, ~62 vol % in fcc) and secondary γ* (A1 structure, several nm to tens of nm).; Average spacing between adjacent γ′ nanoprecipitates is ~11 nm.; Dislocations were observed to shear both the primary γ′ and secondary γ* precipitates during in situ TEM compression.; Grain diameters average ~409 nm for the fcc phase and ~227 nm for the bcc phase.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is primarily attributed to precipitation strengthening via the shearing mechanism, where dislocations shear both the primary coherent γ′ precipitates and the secondary coherent γ* precipitates, creating an 'exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect' due to the hierarchical obstacle distribution. Additional contributions come from grain-boundary strengthening (due to submicrometer grains) and load transfer via the hard bcc phase.. Limitations: The chemical composition of the secondary γ* precipitates could not be obtained due to their very small sizes.. Future work: The authors suggest the design strategy provides insight for achieving ultrahigh strength in HEAs or other multicomponent alloys, implying further exploration of hierarchical architectures, though specific future experiments are not explicitly detailed beyond the general validation of the strategy.. Quote: "Here, we report a strategy for the design and fabrication of HEAs that can achieve ultrahigh tensile strengths."

W2896718190.title: A high-entropy alloy with hierarchical nanoprecipitates and ultrahigh strength

card: Paper card. Question: How can nanoprecipitates be designed and controlled in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to achieve high strength while maintaining good ductility, and what are the specific mechanisms governing their formation and strengthening effects?. System: FCC-based HEAs including (FeCoNiCr)94Ti2Al4, Ni2CoCrFeNb0.15, Al0.3Cu0.5CrFeNi2, CoCrFeNi(Ni3Al)x, and (Ni1.5FeCoCr0.5)87.5Al7.5Ti5.0; also BCC-based systems like AlxCoCrCuFeNi and refractory systems like TaNbHfZrTi. Processing: Aging heat treatments at temperatures ranging from 550 °C to 1000 °C for durations from 150 h to 720 h; severe plastic deformation for grain refinement; mechanical alloying (MA) for high-density particle introduction; laser cladding for coatings; and direct addition of stoichiometric strengthening phases (e.g., Ni3Al) to the matrix. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing; compression testing; corrosion testing in NaCl and sulfuric acid solutions; hardness measurements (HV); microstructural analysis via TEM/SEM after aging; cryogenic treatment at -40 °C. Findings: The Ni2CoCrFeNb0.15 HEA aged at 650 °C for 80 h retained D022-Ni3Nb precipitates with a size of only ≈15 nm, demonstrating the slow diffusion effect in HEAs.; The (FeCoNiCr)94Ti2Al4 HEA achieved a yield strength of ≈1005 MPa and tensile strength of ≈1,273 MPa with an elongation of ≈17% due to nanoprecipitate strengthening.; In the Al0.3Cu0.5CrFeNi2 HEA, adding 0.073 at% C promoted M23C6 carbide formation, increasing yield strength by 193 MPa and ultimate tensile strength by 415 MPa while maintaining 88% elongation.; The (Ni1.5FeCoCr0.5)87.5Al7.5Ti5.0 HEA exhibited a yield strength >1.0 GPa, tensile strength ≈1.5 GPa, and elongation ≈50% due to a unique nanolamellar structure with coherent boundaries.; The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA aged at 800 °C showed a precipitate size increase of only 6 nm (from 45 nm to 51 nm) between 50 h and 100 h aging, indicating slow coarsening.; In the CoCrFeNiMo0.3 alloy, the precipitation of fine σ and μ intermetallic phases resulted in a yield strength of 816 MPa, tensile strength of 1.2 GPa, and elongation of 19%.; The γ′ phase in HEAs can be stabilized by adjusting the Ti/Al ratio; a ratio within 0.7–2 favors L12 phase formation, while Ti/Al = 1/3 favors B2 phase formation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior performance to the 'slow diffusion' effect in HEAs, which limits precipitate growth and coarsening, allowing for the retention of fine nanoscale precipitates. Strengthening mechanisms include Orowan bypass for incoherent large precipitates, dislocation cutting for coherent nanoscale precipitates (L12, D022), order strengthening due to atomic arrangement, and grain refinement strengthening where carbides suppress grain growth. The 'cocktail effect' and high mixing entropy also contribute to phase stability and the formation of simple solid solutions.. Limitations: The text states that the influence of the size and type of nanoprecipitates on the strengthening effect is still not clear, and the design method and precipitation conditions are relatively vague. Additionally, increasing the volume fraction of γ′ precipitates can increase the risk of forming harmful intermetallic compounds or cause processing problems. Over-aging can lead to the transformation of metastable phases into hard, brittle intermetallic compounds (like δ, σ, or η phases), which deteriorate mechanical properties.. Future work: The authors outline the need to further explore the effects of the types and sizes of nanoprecipitates on the strengthening effect. They propose using the OVEC (valence electron concentration) design strategy to control precipitate structures. Future work should focus on alloy-design strategies that consider the matrix composition after precipitates separate out, rather than just the initial composition, to maintain the advantages of HEAs.. Quote: "The characteristics of multiple principal elements and slow diffusion effect of elements in HEAs provide a chance to form fine and stable nanoscale precipitates, pushing the strengths of the alloys to new high levels."

Paper card. Question: How can new nanoprecipitates and strengthening mechanisms be designed to achieve high strength without sacrificing ductility in high-entropy alloys, and what are the specific characteristics required for these precipitates and their matrix?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (FCC matrix with L12 γ' and γ* phases), Al0.7CoCrFeNi (B2 phase with Cr-rich BCC precipitates), Al0.2CrFeCoNi2Cu0.2, lightweight Al1.5CrFeMnTi (BCC matrix with L21 phase), and refractory (TiZrHfNb)98O2. Processing: Aging treatments at temperatures between 600 and 800 °C; specific examples include aging at 700 °C for 20 h or 800 °C for 1 h; solution aging followed by direct aging; annealing to change size, shape, and coherency of L21 phases; addition of 2.0 at% O to TaNbHfZrTi. Test conditions: Aging temperatures ranging from 550 to 800 °C; aging times of 1 h to 20 h; tensile testing at room temperature (yield strength 1.11 ± 0.03 GPa, ductility 27.66% ± 1.13%); diffusion couple experiments at 1273–1373 K. Findings: The Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 HEA with Ω = 1.119 and δ = 6.277 generated a γ′ phase with an L12 structure in a disordered FCC matrix.; In dual-phase FCC + B2 structures, ellipsoidal-ordered L12 precipitates with a diameter of 8 nm were observed in FCC dendrites, while BCC-structured precipitates with a diameter around 10 nm were observed in B2 dendrites.; The precipitation temperature of γ′ nano-precipitates is between 600 and 800 °C, which is higher than that of other γ′ phases (500–750 °C).; In Al0.2CrFeCoNi2Cu0.2, the L12 phase was present after aging at 700 °C for 20 h, but no nanoscale precipitation occurred after 1 h at 800 °C.; Re-precipitation of the Laves phase was detected inside grains and on grain boundaries in solution-aging samples, whereas direct-aging samples only contained γ and γ′ phases.; The tensile yield strength of the (TiZrHfNb)98O2 refractory HEA reached 1.11 ± 0.03 GPa with a tensile ductility of 27.66% ± 1.13%.; Cu-rich nanoprecipitates precipitate around 700 °C with slower kinetics compared to the L12-ordered phase.; Carbides exhibit a much wider precipitation temperature range (550–800 °C) and are more stable than other precipitates.. Mechanism: Small lattice mismatch between nanoprecipitates and the matrix reduces specific interface energy, stabilizing nanoscale size; high shear modulus and antiphase-domain-boundary energy hinder dislocation cutting, providing coherent, modulus, and ordered strengthening; high number density is achieved via low driving force of nucleation and matrix defects; twin boundaries and phase-transformation-induced plasticity absorb dislocations to improve plasticity; nanoprecipitates act as traps for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.. Limitations: Comprehensive mechanical properties do not yet reach full potentials; almost all effective nanoprecipitates are derived from superalloys with no unique HEA-specific precipitates found; negative effects include nanoprecipitate coarsening or crystal-structure transformation during high-temperature service; matrix phase design for functional properties often fails to meet expected comprehensive mechanical properties simultaneously.. Future work: Explore new nanoprecipitates and strengthening mechanisms that enhance strength without sacrificing ductility; investigate the slow diffusion effect in HEAs to better understand nucleation and growth of precipitates; study the interactions between intrinsic heterogeneities and precipitates; introduce nanoprecipitates into lightweight, refractory, and radiation-resistant HEA systems; utilize high-density dislocations and modulated FCC-to-BCC transformations for strengthening.. Quote: "The new type of nanoprecipitates should exhibit a strength enhancement without scarifying the ductility."

Question: Can CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy coatings, produced via mechanical alloying and electro spark deposition, provide effective corrosion resistance and adhesion for stainless steel substrates in aggressive geothermal environments?. System: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy deposited on 316 L stainless steel substrate. Processing: Solid-state processing: Mechanical alloying of high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Mo powders for 30 h in a Pulverisette 6 Classic Line planetary ball mill (350 RPM, ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, N-Heptane process control agent) under Argon; cold pressing at 250 kN into 25 mm × 5 mm samples; sintering at 1100 °C for 1 h; machining into electrodes; electro spark deposition (ESD) under Argon atmosphere to deposit successive layers.. Test conditions: Pull-off testing per ASTM D4541–01; electrochemical corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 ± 0.5 °C for 6 h using potentiodynamic polarization.. Findings: Maximum adhesion resistance reached 0.67 MPa, limited by epoxy resin failure rather than coating-substrate interface failure.; Corrosion rate of the ESD coating calculated at 0.00016 mm/year in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.; Polarization resistance of the coating was higher than 316 L stainless steel (22.50 kΩ × cm2).; XRD analysis revealed an increase in σ phase (rich in Co, Cr, Fe) and μ phase (rich in Mo) in the coating compared to the sintered electrode.; The coating microstructure showed a homogeneous and adhesive layer near the substrate, with slight porosity and splats in the upper part.; After corrosion testing, a passivation layer formed on the surface, covering most pores, containing an oxygen component likely from segregated chromium.; The open circuit potential (Eoc) was more electronegative than the bulk as-cast alloy, attributed to increased porosity delaying passivation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the phase transformation (increase in σ and μ phases) to the rapid melting and cooling during the electro spark deposition process, driven by temperature differences and local solute solidification. The superior corrosion resistance is explained by the rapid formation of a passivation film, likely containing segregated chromium, which covers surface pores and reduces the corrosion current density significantly compared to bulk alloys or stainless steel.. Limitations: The coating is slightly porous in the upper part due to the BCC structure prone to pore formation in this high-entropy alloy and the ESD technique; the open circuit potential is more electronegative than the bulk alloy due to this porosity delaying passivation.. Future work: The authors state that novel promising coatings resistant to long-term high-temperature oxidation, corrosion action, and wear are currently being sought, implying further development is needed for these specific conditions.. card: Paper card. Question: How does the machinability of Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy compare to 304 stainless steel in terms of cutting forces, tool wear, surface quality, and microstructural changes during milling?. System: Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) and X5CrNi18-10 (304) stainless steel. Processing: Face milling using a 12 mm diameter shank cutter with two indexable carbide inserts (grade HSC 05, PVTi coating) on a FIRST MCV 300 vertical milling center; dry cutting conditions; 25 tests using Taguchi method with cutting speed (vc), feed per tooth (fz), and axial depth of cut (ap) varied; radial depth of cut ae = 12 mm (100%); sample dimensions 145 × 15 × 6 mm³ for HEA. Test conditions: Dry cutting; spindle speeds up to 8000 rpm; feed rates up to 103 mm/min; axial depth of cut (ap) ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.42 mm; feed per tooth (fz) ranging from 0.05 mm/tooth to 0.15 mm/tooth; cutting speed (vc) varied across 5 levels; temperature measured via thermo vision camera (0–500 °C range); cutting forces measured with Kistler 9257B dynamometer. Findings: The machinability of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of 304 stainless steel based on the resultant cutting force.; Cutting temperatures ranged from 120 °C to 281 °C, with the maximum temperature (213.2 °C) recorded after about 6 s of processing.; The axial depth of cut (ap) was identified as the main influencing parameter on cutting temperature, with maximum temperatures (240–281 °C) occurring at ap = 0.42 mm.; Maximum flank wear width (VBB max) was 86 µm for the first cutting edge (CE1) and 67 µm for the second cutting edge (CE2).; Maximum crater dimensions on the rack face for CE2 were KBmax = 490 µm and KMmax = 225 µm.; Surface roughness values ranged from 0.39 µm to 2.058 µm, with the best values obtained at minimum feed (fz = 0.05 mm/tooth).; Microhardness of the machined HEA surfaces ranged from 365 HV0.2 to 444 HV0.2, attributed to material inhomogeneity and self-hardening.; XRD analysis showed that patterns for as-cast and machined surfaces were very similar, with no new phases formed during machining.. Mechanism: The superior machinability of the HEA compared to stainless steel is attributed to its specific cutting force behavior, where the resultant force is lower despite higher hardness. The irregular chip fragmentation and surface defects are caused by the inhomogeneity of the cast material and the presence of hard intermetallic phases (e.g., Fe2Al5, FeAl3) which act as micro-edges causing tool wear. Self-hardening effects and oxidation during cutting contribute to the increased microhardness and chip fragmentation, while the similar XRD patterns indicate the material withstands heating cycles without phase transformation.. Limitations: The study was limited to dry cutting conditions and did not evaluate the effects of cooling and lubrication. The research is described as preliminary, and the number of reference XRD patterns available in the database is limited. The study did not cover extended ranges of cutting parameters for finish and rough cuts, nor did it generate predictive mathematical models for material removal rate or tool life.. Future work: More detailed research should be achieved to have a more precise image of the machinability of the HEA by considering the cutting speed, material removal rate and cutting tool life. Furthermore, extended ranges of the cutting parameters should be considered for both finish cut and rough cut and to generate predictive mathematical models to improve processing and optimize cutting parameters.. Quote: "In terms of cutting forces, the behavior of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of stainless steel."

card: Paper card. Question: Does the equiatomic AlAgCuNiSnTi alloy meet the criteria for a high entropy alloy, and what are its microstructural, thermal, and corrosion properties?. System: AlAgCuNiSnTi equiatomic multicomponent alloy (six elements in equal atomic concentrations). Processing: Vacuum Arc Remelting (VAR) using MRF-ABJ900 equipment under argon atmosphere; five remelting cycles; samples also processed via melt spinning to obtain ~1 mm thick strips; homogenization heat treatment at 800 °C. Test conditions: Microhardness measured with FM-700 AHOTEC tester (HV0.1/15); thermal analysis via DTA and DIL at 10 °C/min heating/cooling rates; corrosion testing in 3.5% NaCl solution using potentiodynamic method with BioLogic SP-150. Findings: The alloy does not meet high entropy alloy criteria; ΔHmix = −10.13 kJ/mol and δ = 8.92 place it in the intermediate phase alloy range.; The as-cast microstructure is three-phase (four phases identified by XRD: TiNiSn, Ag3Sn, Al1.33Cu0.67, and Sn5Ti6).; Average microhardness of the as-cast alloy is 487 HV0.1/15, with the TiNi1.056Sn phase reaching a maximum of 600 HV0.1/15.; The corrosion rate stabilizes at 0.004 mm/y after initial passivation in 3.5% NaCl solution.; The corrosion rate (0.004 mm/y) is better than FeNiCoMnCrAl (0.009 mm/y) and FeNiCoMnCr (0.226 mm/y) HEAs in the same solution.; Homogenization at 800 °C did not cause major changes in the microstructure, though it slightly decreased hardness.; Melt spinning produced ~1 mm thick strips with a more homogeneous and grain-refined microstructure compared to the cast ingot.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the alloy forms intermediate phases rather than a single solid solution due to thermodynamic parameters (ΔHmix and δ) falling outside the high entropy alloy range. The high corrosion resistance is attributed to the positive action of titanium oxide forming a passivation layer on the surface.. Limitations: The alloy does not meet the criteria to be classified as a high entropy alloy; it contains multiple phases (intermetallics) rather than a single solid solution structure.. Future work: The authors propose that the alloy can be used for surface coating applications due to its high corrosion resistance.. Quote: "The results show that the as-cast alloy microstructure is three-phase, with an average microhardness of 487 HV0.1/15."

card: Paper card. Question: How do laser metal deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings perform regarding erosion and corrosion resistance in three distinct geothermal environments, and how do manufacturing defects influence their degradation?. System: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 (Mo-HEA) and Al0.5CoCrFeNi (Al-HEA) coatings deposited on carbon steel (S235JR) and stainless steel (AISI 316L, 304L) substrates. Processing: Laser metal deposition (LMD) using a Trumpf Trudisk 8002 5.3 kW disc laser system, Reis RV60-40 robot, and Oerlikon-Metco 10-C powder feeder under argon atmosphere; coating thickness 800–1000 µm; no post-deposition grinding or polishing. Test conditions: Three environments at Hellisheidi geothermal site: (1) Wellhead test at 194 °C and 14 bar (deaerated); (2) Aerated test at 90 °C and 1 bar (fluid mixed with atmospheric gas); (3) Erosion test at 198 °C and 15 bar (high-velocity fluid impact at 90° angle). Findings: Mo-HEA coatings on carbon steel exhibited manufacturing cracks up to 50–60 µm deep, while Mo-HEA on stainless steel showed no cracks.; Al-HEA coatings were prone to general and localized corrosion damage in all tests, forming oxide-rich films 20–40 µm thick in the wellhead test.; In the erosion test, Al-HEA coatings developed erosion pits deeper than 100 µm after a 90-day exposure period.; Erosion pits in Mo-HEA coatings were observed only at the location of pre-existing vertical cracks, where fluid turbulence increased damage.; Mo-HEA coatings on stainless steel substrates showed no adhesion damage or cracking in any of the three test environments.; Galvanic corrosion products (iron-based) formed at the interface of Mo-HEA coatings and carbon steel substrates after exposure and ambient drying.; The oxide layer on Mo-HEA in the aerated test was discontinuous, likely due to Cr concentration gradients and sluggish diffusion rates.. Mechanism: Manufacturing cracks in Mo-HEA on carbon steel induce fluid turbulence that accelerates erosion; Al-HEA suffers from internal stresses and rapid oxidation kinetics of Al leading to non-passive, brittle oxide films; galvanic effects between noble Mo-HEA and carbon steel exacerbate corrosion at interfaces upon exposure to ambient air.. Limitations: The study notes that surface roughness measurements were inconclusive due to scaling dominance, and the statistical null hypothesis method for erosion assessment failed due to high variability in coating thickness.. Future work: The formulation and production of the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating need to be optimized to prevent cracking on carbon steel substrates; longer exposure periods are needed to verify if the discontinuous oxide layer on Mo-HEA becomes continuous.. Quote: "Wide manufacturing cracks are concluded to enhance the fluid-induced erosion effect for the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating in the vicinity of the cracks."

card: Paper card. Question: How does temperature influence the superplasticity, strengthening mechanisms, and deformation behavior of CoNiCrFeMn high entropy alloy nanowires compared to single-component Ag nanowires?. System: CoNiCrFeMn equiatomic high entropy alloy (20 at.% each) and single-element Ag nanowires. Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS; nanowires extracted from bulk FCC along [110] with circular (110) cross-section; equilibrated at 77, 300, and 1000 K; constant strain rate of 10^8 1/s applied in NVT ensemble. Test conditions: Tensile deformation at 77 K, 300 K, and 1000 K; strain rate 10^8 1/s; Ag NW (47,250 atoms); HEA NW (55,216 atoms). Findings: At 77 K, Ag NWs exhibit superplasticity via (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation driven by partial dislocation nucleation and twin boundary propagation.; CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs reach a peak stress of ~6.2 GPa at 5–6% elongation at 77 K, showing serration behavior due to Lomer Cottrell lock formation.; At 77 K, HEA NWs achieve ~45% elongation to fracture due to synergistic TWIP (twinning induced plasticity) and TRIP (transformation induced plasticity) mechanisms.; At 300 K, HEA NWs maintain a flow stress of ~5.5 GPa at 5% strain with simultaneous partial dislocation nucleation and deformation twinning.; At 1000 K, HEA NWs maintain good flow stress and ductility, with FCC-HCP martensitic transformation dominating and HCP phase fraction increasing rapidly.; Dislocation density is highest at 77 K and decreases with increasing temperature, shifting the dominant mechanism from TWIP to TRIP.; Lomer Cottrell locks in HEA NWs act as barriers at low temperatures but are unlocked/annihilated by HCP phase formation at high temperatures.. Mechanism: The exceptional strength-ductility trade-off in HEA nanowires arises from the synergistic interaction of twinning induced plasticity (TWIP), transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) via FCC-HCP martensitic transformation, and cross-section reorientation. At low temperatures, lattice distortion and friction hinder partial dislocation motion, promoting Lomer Cottrell lock formation which enhances work hardening. At high temperatures, thermal energy facilitates the unlocking of these locks via HCP phase accumulation, enabling continued plasticity and refractory properties.. Limitations: The study is based on molecular dynamics simulations with a specific strain rate (10^8 1/s) and does not account for experimental synthesis challenges or long-term stability under different strain rates.. Future work: The findings could be useful for designing nanowires at different temperatures with high stability and superior mechanical properties in the semiconductor industry.. Quote: "HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: What alloying and scaling conditions lead to the strongest both ductile and stable materials?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) thin films and pillars. Processing: d.c. magnetron co-sputtering on (100) silicon or sapphire substrates at room temperature; Ion beam-assisted deposition (IBAD) used with 1.2 keV beam energy, 5 mA current, and 35° incidence angle to reduce grain size; Focused Ga ion beams (FIB) used to mill pillars with diameters of ~1 μm, 500, 200, and 100 nm. Test conditions: Microcompression tests at a strain rate of 2 × 10−3 s−1; Thermal annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days in argon atmosphere. Findings: HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ~10 GPa, one order of magnitude higher than the bulk form.; Compressive plastic strains over 30% were achieved in smaller pillars without cracking.; 580-nm Normal HEA pillars show a yield strength of ~5 GPa, while 580-nm IBAD HEA pillars reach ~6.5 GPa.; Smallest IBAD HEA pillars (~70–100 nm diameter) exhibit yield strengths of ~8–10 GPa.; After annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days, HEA pillars retain a high yield strength of ~5 GPa, whereas pure W films show significant grain growth and pore formation.; IBAD HEA pillars exhibit a log–log slope of −0.2 for the relationship between flow stress and pillar diameter, indicating the lowest size dependence among reported pillars.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is attributed to the simultaneous operation of four strengthening mechanisms: lattice friction, Taylor hardening, source-controlled strength, and grain-boundary strengthening. The excellent thermal stability is attributed to relatively low grain-boundary energy due to the highly disordered grain interiors in HEAs, which lowers the driving force for grain-boundary migration compared to pure metals.. Limitations: The text notes that large pillars (>1 μm) experience cracking at strains larger than ~20% and that the smallest pillars (~70–100 nm) show higher scattering levels in strength due to inhomogeneous distribution of grain boundaries.. Future work: The authors state that mechanical tests for small-scale HEAs at high temperatures are still needed to prove their capability as high-temperature materials, and that further work is required to optimize small-scale HEAs for applications, such as determining the best alloying elements and optimized grain and specimen size combinations.. Quote: "Here we report a strategy for the fabrication of refractory HEA thin films and small-sized pillars that consist of strongly textured, columnar and nanometre-sized grains."

card: Paper card. Question: How local chemistry affects enhanced deformation mechanisms and the origin of strain hardening in dual-phase high-entropy alloys.. System: Cantor-like Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 high-entropy alloy (at.%) comprising face-centered cubic (fcc) austenite and hexagonal closed packed (hcp) ε-martensite phases.. Processing: Vacuum induction casting of 4-kg ingots, hot rolling at 900 °C (50% reduction), homogenization at 1200 °C for 3 h with water quenching, cold rolling to 40–50% thickness reduction, and recrystallization annealing at 800 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1); in situ TEM straining at ambient temperature (200 kV, loading rate ~1 μm/s); nanoscale pillar compression (300 nm diameter, 2 nm/s displacement rate).. Findings: The alloy exhibits a tensile strength approaching 1 GPa and ductility of almost 60% at ambient temperatures.; Partial dislocation activities result in stable three-dimensional stacking-fault networks comprising multiple stacking faults and sessile Lomer–Cottrell locks.; The fraction of the stronger hcp phase progressively increases during plastic deformation by forming at the stacking-fault network boundaries in the fcc phase.; Dual-phase pillars displayed the highest ultimate strength at ~3.45 GPa, compared to ~2.25 GPa for pure hcp and ~1.25 GPa for pure fcc pillars.; Local chemical composition variations show Ni atomic fraction fluctuating from −58% to 115% about its average, with Mn near stacking faults being nearly 30% higher than in the matrix.; The continuous fcc → hcp phase transformation sustains a hardening effect where flow stress increases two-fold from 1.75 to ~3.5 GPa.; Lomer–Cottrell locks act to immobilize dislocation motion and provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation.. Mechanism: The authors argue that variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of stable 3D stacking-fault networks. These networks impede dislocation motion (work hardening) and serve as preferred sites for the nucleation and growth of the hcp phase via a transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, where the continuous increase in the hcp volume fraction drives the ultrahigh strain hardening.. Limitations: The fracture toughness of these TRIP HEAs may not be similarly enhanced compared to the Cantor alloy, particularly at decreasing temperatures, because the product hcp ε-martensite phase tends to be quite brittle.. Future work: The authors propose that the intentional generation of Lomer–Cottrell locks raises a fundamental question of how to increase the probability of interactions between dissociated dislocations with the sole objective of enhancing the formation of such locks.. Quote: "variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of the stacking-fault networks to provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation."

W2776853557.title: Anomalous Tensile Detwinning in Twinned Nanowires

card: Paper card. Question: How does aluminum addition and temperature variation affect the generalized stacking fault energy (GSFE) and twinning ability of face-centered cubic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys?. System: fcc Aly(CrMnFeCoNi)100−y where y = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Processing: First-principles calculations using the exact muffin-tin orbitals (EMTO) method with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional and coherent-potential approximation (CPA); paramagnetic state modeled via disordered local magnetic moment approach; lattice constants derived from experimental data and thermal expansion coefficients.. Test conditions: Temperature range covering room temperature up to 600 K; Al concentrations of 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 at.%; paramagnetic state assumed.. Findings: At room temperature for the Al-free alloy, intrinsic stacking fault energy (γisf) is -6 mJ/m² and extrinsic stacking fault energy (γesf) is 3 mJ/m².; Unstable stacking fault energy (γusf) and unstable twinning fault energy (γutf) are 285 mJ/m² and 281 mJ/m² respectively at room temperature.; Both γisf and γesf increase monotonously with increasing temperature and Al content.; Both γusf and γutf decrease monotonously with increasing temperature and Al content.; The hcp-fcc interfacial energy (σ) remains in the range of 4–7 mJ/m² and is weakly dependent on temperature and Al content.; Two twinning ability parameters (Ttw and rd) indicate that twinability decreases with increasing temperature or Al content.; The alloys remain prone to twinning even at 600 K and 8% Al content, as Ttw remains far above 1.; Negative γisf values are observed for the Al-free alloy below 400 K, consistent with the thermodynamic stability of the hcp phase at low temperatures.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the negative γisf at low temperatures to the thermodynamic stability of the hexagonal close packed (hcp) phase relative to the fcc phase. The increase in γisf with temperature and Al content is linked to the changing free energy difference between hcp and fcc lattices, while the decrease in unstable fault energies is observed as a monotonic trend. The interfacial energy is derived from the difference between the calculated γisf and the structural energy difference (γ0), showing weak dependence on composition and temperature.. Limitations: The study notes that the current twinning parameter (rd) cannot explain the observation of deformation twins in Al-free CrMnFeCoNi HEA below 400 K where the parameter predicts only stacking fault and full slip. Additionally, the authors state that predicting whether twinning is realized at elevated temperatures depends crucially on alloy preparation, microstructure, and strain rate, which are not captured by the current intrinsic energy parameters.. Future work: The authors propose that further theory is needed to resolve the discrepancy between the twinning parameter predictions and experimental observations at low temperatures. They also suggest that describing the effects of alloy preparation, microstructure, and strain rate requires further advanced models built upon the disclosed intrinsic energy parameters.. Quote: "Upon Al addition or temperature increase, the intrinsic and extrinsic stacking fault energies increase, whereas the unstable stacking fault and unstable twinning fault energies decrease monotonously."
