card: Paper card. Question: How does modifying grain boundary morphology from straight to serrated affect the hot ductility drop, tensile fracture strain, and creep rupture life of a selective laser melting (SLM) fabricated precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures?. System: Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%) high-entropy alloy (SLMHEA) with fcc γ matrix and L12 γ′ precipitates. Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) with 270 W laser power, 1000 mm/s scanning speed, 75 μm hatch distance, and 200°C pre-heat; followed by solution heat treatment at 1120°C for 1 h; HT-1 involved air-cooling to room temperature then aging at 750°C for 48 h; HT-2 involved slow cooling at 1°C/min to 1000°C then air-cooling to room temperature followed by aging at 750°C for 48 h. Test conditions: Tensile tests at 25°C and 650°C with strain rate 10−3 s−1; creep tests at 650°C/650 MPa; molecular dynamic simulations at 650°C under 650 MPa load. Findings: Serrated grain boundary increased tensile fracture strain at 650°C by a factor of 3.5 (from 1.8% to 6.3%); Serrated grain boundary increased creep rupture life at 650°C/650 MPa by a factor of 400 (from 0.58 h to 274 h); Minimum creep strain rate decreased by 96% in the serrated sample (from 6.4 × 10−6 s−1 to 2.4 × 10−7 s−1); Average strain at triple junctions reduced from 28% in straight grain boundaries to 11% in serrated grain boundaries (reduction >50%); HT-2 sample (serrated) exhibited 0.45% creep fracture strain compared to 0.03% for HT-1 (straight); Grain boundary serration wavelength was 3.29 ± 0.38 μm and amplitude was 1.69 ± 0.24 μm in HT-2 samples; Coarse γ′ precipitates in HT-2 had an average size of 1.8 μm, compared to 60.1 nm in HT-1; Geometric factor ϕ for creep rate calculation was 0.017 for serrated boundaries versus 1 for straight boundaries. Mechanism: The slow cooling process coarsens L12 γ′ precipitates which interact with mobile grain boundaries via the Zener drag effect, pinning them and causing undulation (serration). This serrated morphology distributes strains more evenly, reduces local strain concentration at triple junctions by over 50%, acts as a crack deflector to retard intergranular crack propagation, and provides resistance against shear parallel to the grain boundary surface.. Limitations: The thermodynamic database predictions for σ phase, C14 Laves phase, B2 phase, and borides did not match experimental observations, likely due to database inaccuracies or non-equilibrium conditions; the study focuses on a single alloy composition and specific heat treatment parameters.. card: Paper card. Question: How can a hierarchical microstructure be induced in a single crystal high entropy superalloy (HESA) to achieve superior high-temperature tensile yield strength and ductility compared to advanced single crystal superalloys?. System: Ni48.3Co16.9Al10.2Fe8.9Cr7.4Ti5.8Nb1.2Mo0.9W0.4 (at.%) single crystal high entropy superalloy (HESA). Processing: Bridgman casting of single crystal bars; HT-1: single ramp from room temperature to 1,500 K in 20 h followed by air cooling; HT-2: HT-1 followed by additional heat treatment at 1,023 K for 20 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Tensile tests conducted at 298 K, 723 K, 923 K, 1,023 K, and 1,173 K with a constant strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: HESA in HT-2 state achieved a tensile yield strength of 1,023 MPa at 1,023 K, which is 110 MPa higher than CMSX-4.; The cost-specific yield strength of HESA is 8 times that of CMSX-4.; HESA exhibited a tensile elongation greater than 20% at 1,023 K, which is three times greater than that of CMSX-4.; The HT-2 microstructure contains a dispersion of nano-sized disordered FCC particles (4 nm radius, 4.3 vol%) inside ordered L12 precipitates.; The presence of nano HE-FCC particles contributed an estimated 110 MPa increase in yield strength compared to the HT-1 state.; The average L12 precipitate size increased from 143 nm in HT-1 to 153 nm in HT-2.; At 1,173 K, the HE-FCC particles disappeared, and the yield strength of HT-1 and HT-2 states became similar.; The raw material cost of HESA is 84% cheaper than CMSX-4 due to the absence of Re element content.. Mechanism: The formation of nano-sized disordered FCC particles inside the ordered L12 precipitates is driven by the supersaturation of FCC phase formers within the L12 phase during the HT-1 cooling process; these particles act as obstacles that pin superdislocations, increasing the energy required for dislocation motion and thereby enhancing yield strength.. Limitations: The metastable FCC particles inside the L12 phase are thermodynamically unstable and tend to dissolve into the surrounding FCC matrix after prolonged ageing (e.g., 200 h at 1,023 K) or at higher temperatures (1,173 K), leading to a loss of the hierarchical strengthening effect.. Future work: Future alloy design should utilize slow-diffusing species such as Mo to prolong the dissolution rate of FCC particles and improve the thermal stability of the hierarchical microstructure for creep resistance.. Quote: "A hierarchical microstructure strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with superior cost specific yield strength from room temperature up to 1,023 K is presented."

card: Paper card. Question: How can single-phase refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) be designed to achieve ultrahigh yield strength at 1600°C, and what is the underlying deformation mechanism responsible for the observed plateau strength?. System: Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). Processing: Vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization treatment at 2100°C for 2 hours with subsequent air cooling in an ultrahigh-temperature furnace under Ar flow. Test conditions: Compression testing at a strain rate of 10⁻³ 1/s from ambient temperature to 1600°C; samples were 3.6 mm in diameter and 6 mm in height for 1600°C tests. Findings: HfMoNbTaW alloy after homogenization exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, which is higher than MoNbTaVW (477 MPa).; A plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C for HfMoNbTaW, with a value of approximately 950 MPa.; Homogenization at 2100°C for 2 h results in a homogeneous body-centered cubic (bcc) phase with no precipitation.; The theoretical yield strength (σycal) for HfMoNbTaW increases by 30.8% from 2393 MPa to 3131 MPa upon equiatomic addition of Hf into MoNbTaW.; The shear modulus of HfMoNbTaW was measured to be 73 ± 1 GPa via nanoindentation.; Extrapolation of high-temperature strength data suggests a room temperature strength of 4536 MPa, consistent with edge dislocation control calculations (4206 MPa).; Adding Hf to MoNbTaW increases yield strength by 47.5% compared to MoNbTaW (1561 MPa vs 1058 MPa).. Mechanism: The authors propose that the plateau strength and ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength result from a transition in the deformation mode from screw dislocations to edge dislocations. Below the critical temperature (Tc), strength decreases due to thermal activation of screw dislocations. Above Tc, edge dislocations become dominant in general yielding, leading to a plateau in strength and high strength at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The text notes that the theoretical yield strength calculated using the average shear modulus (Gmix) is generally larger than the experimental value, and that the assumption of mixed dislocation control (α=9) was an overestimate compared to screw dislocation control (α=2) at low temperatures.. Future work: The authors state that a similar alloy design strategy could be applied to develop more RHEAs with an ultrahigh strength level.. Quote: "HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa)."

W2992394995.title: High entropy alloys: A focused review of mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the individual effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on the microstructure and mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and elevated-temperature performance) of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory high-entropy alloys?. System: Equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr and its five sub-alloys created by the subtraction method: HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi. Processing: Vacuum-arc melting of 99.9 wt.% (99.99 wt.% for Ti) pure elements stacked by melting point, re-melted at least four times, and solidified in a water-cool copper mold. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature, 800 °C, 1000 °C, 1200 °C, and 1400 °C; crosshead speed 0.36 mm/min (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); cylindrical samples 3.6 mm diameter x 6 mm height. Findings: HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy yield strength was 1512 MPa at room temperature and 556 MPa at 1200 °C.; HfMoTaTiZr (Nb removed) showed the highest room temperature yield strength of 1600 MPa but lower toughness.; HfMoNbTaTi (Zr removed) exhibited the best comprehensive properties with 27% fracture strain at room temperature and 367 MPa yield strength at 1400 °C.; The presence of Mo increased room temperature yield strength from 929 MPa (in HfNbTaTiZr) to 1512 MPa but reduced fracture strain from >50% to 12%.; Nb addition increased yield strength by 38% at 1200 °C and significantly improved room temperature fracture strain.; Zr addition increased strength but strongly deteriorated room temperature toughness, reducing fracture strain from 27% to 12%.; Alloys with Mo present showed much better strength at elevated temperatures compared to HfNbTaTiZr.; At 1200 °C, HfMoNbTaTi alloy had the highest specific strength among the tested alloys.. Mechanism: The high yield strength is attributed to the solid solution strengthening effect driven by atomic size and shear modulus mismatch; the high entropy effect promotes the formation of a single BCC disordered solid solution phase despite binary phase diagrams suggesting intermetallics; severe lattice distortion reduces the effective shear modulus by approximately 30% compared to the rule of mixtures.. Limitations: There is a deviation of about 30% between calculated and experimental yield strengths, likely due to overestimated shear modulus; the criteria for Laves phase formation were not fully consistent with experimental observations; the reduction in shear modulus due to lattice distortion requires further research to confirm reasons.. Future work: Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are required for high-temperature applications in air; more research is needed to confirm the elemental effects in other RHEA systems and to understand the reasons for reduced shear modulus.. Quote: "The subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element"

card: Paper card. Question: How does a novel refractory high entropy alloy (NV1) behave under long-term isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C and 1100 °C, and what is the mechanism governing its oxidation resistance over 200 hours?. System: NV1 alloy (Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, Ti; designed based on CrMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr with reduced Ti, removed Zr, and added Al, Si, increased Cr). Processing: Cold crucible levitation melting of high purity elemental raw materials (>99.9 wt%) to cast a 1.1 kg cone-shaped ingot; samples machined by electrical discharge machining and ground to 1200 grit; isothermal oxidation performed in flowing dry air using a thermogravimetric analyser (SETARAM TAG 24-18S) and muffle furnace. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours in flowing dry air; microstructural characterization performed at intervals of 1, 12, 40, 50, 100, and 200 hours. Findings: At 1000 °C, the mass gain after 200 hours was 6.53 mg/cm2, following an exponential dependence throughout the entire duration.; At 1100 °C, the mass gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which is lower than at 1000 °C, showing three stages of parabolic dependence.; The external oxide layer at both temperatures consisted primarily of a CrTaO4-based oxide with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3.; At 1000 °C, the CrTaO4-based oxide layer was porous with large volume defects due to insufficient kinetics, preventing it from acting as an effective barrier.; At 1100 °C, the CrTaO4-based oxide layer was denser and more continuous, leading to controlled oxidation and reduced weight gain.; TiN particles (size ~1.5 μm) formed preferentially within the Mo-rich dendritic regions at both temperatures, while Al2O3 formed in the internal oxidation depth.; The CrTaO4-based oxide at 1100 °C contained up to 7 at% Al and 2.2 at% less Cr compared to the oxide formed at 1000 °C, indicating non-stoichiometric substitution.. Mechanism: At 1000 °C, insufficient kinetics prevented the formation of a dense, protective CrTaO4 layer, leading to heterogeneous oxidation, volume defects, and exponential weight gain driven by external oxidation and nitridation. At 1100 °C, enhanced diffusion kinetics allowed for the homogeneous growth of a denser, continuous CrTaO4-based layer that acted as a barrier to oxygen and element diffusion, resulting in parabolic weight gain; however, Mo evaporation at the oxide/substrate interface in Stage II temporarily accelerated oxidation before Stage III saw further CrTaO4 formation.. Limitations: The study notes that while CrTaO4-based oxide provided protection, it could not fully prevent the ingestion of oxygen and nitrogen, leading to internal oxidation and nitridation over the long duration.. Future work: The authors propose that the nature of the CrTaO4-based oxide needs to be carefully examined in future studies, and that the influence of nitridation on RHEA properties is an important subject for further investigation.. Quote: "At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2"

card: Paper card. Question: Whether the ordered oxygen complex (OOC) strengthening mechanism, previously observed in high-entropy alloys, can be extended to medium-entropy alloys and how the formation of OOCs can be tailored by adjusting alloy composition.. System: Ti–30Zr–xNb–yO medium-entropy alloys (x = 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30 at.% Nb; y = 0, 1, 2, 3, 3.5, 4 at.% O). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals and TiO2 in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere, followed by remelting at least six times and drop-casting into a water-cooled copper mold (10 × 10 × 60 mm³).. Test conditions: Room-temperature tensile tests at a strain rate of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; internal-friction measurements at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4 Hz with a heating rate of 2 K min⁻¹ from 300 to 1100 K.. Findings: The tensile yield strength of the Ti-30Zr-14Nb-3O MEA was enhanced by ~75% compared to the base alloy.; The elongation of the Ti-30Zr-14Nb-3O MEA was improved by ~164%, reaching ~25.1% compared to ~9.5% for the base alloy.; The number density of OOCs in Ti-30Zr-14Nb-3O was 8.7 × 10²⁴ m⁻³, significantly higher than the 6.7 × 10²³ m⁻³ found in Ti-30Zr-26Nb-3O.; Decreasing the Nb content from 30 at.% to 14 at.% increased the degree of (Ti, Zr)-rich chemical short-range orderings (CSROs).; The percentage of oxygen atoms involved in OOC formation decreased from ~40.9% in Ti-30Zr-14Nb-3O to ~24.0% in Ti-30Zr-30Nb-3O.; Oxygen content exceeding 3.0 at.% (e.g., 4 at.%) caused grain boundary segregation and a transition to intergranular brittle fracture.; The deformation mode shifted from planar slip to wavy slip as the number density of OOCs increased with oxygen doping.. Mechanism: Decreasing phase stability (by reducing Nb content) enhances (Ti, Zr)-rich CSROs, which act as preferential sites for oxygen to occupy octahedral interstitial positions, forming OOCs. These OOCs provide interstitial solid-solution hardening to increase strength and act as dislocation pinning centers that promote cross-slip and wavy slip, thereby enhancing ductility. Excessive oxygen leads to grain boundary segregation, causing embrittlement.. card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be designed to achieve simultaneous high damping capacity, high strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures via Snoek relaxation?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN, and TiO2 in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm x 10 mm x 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, 300 to 1100 K, heating rate 2 K min−1, strain amplitude 2 × 10−4; Mechanical: Room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1. Findings: The O-2 and N-2 HEAs achieved a maximum damping capacity (tanδmax) of 0.020 and 0.027, respectively, at 1.0 Hz.; The damping peak temperature reached up to 800 K, with operating ranges of 60 K, 53 K, and 30 K for the base, O-2, and N-2 HEAs at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a tensile yield strength of 1362 MPa, while the O-2 HEA reached 1138 MPa.; The O-2 HEA displayed a ductility of ~20%, which was double that of the base HEA (~10.8%).; Activation energies for interstitial reorientation were estimated at 2.06 eV (base), 2.40 eV (O-2), and 4.06 eV (N-2).; Approximately 18.5% of oxygen atoms in the O-2 HEA formed ordered oxygen complexes, whereas only ~5.3% of nitrogen atoms in the N-2 HEA formed ordered nitrogen complexes.; The base HEA showed a yield strength of ~810 MPa and a damping capacity of 0.014 at 1.0 Hz.. Mechanism: The high damping capacity originates from Snoek-type relaxation caused by stress-induced position switches of interstitial atoms (oxygen or nitrogen) in the severely distorted bcc lattice. The high strength and ductility are attributed to solid-solution strengthening and ordered interstitial complexes-mediated strain hardening, where the complexes impede dislocation motion and enhance work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the complexity of the alloy composition makes it difficult to conduct a complete peak deconvolution analysis based on all possible individual relaxation processes, and the specific clusters attributing to peaks in the base HEA could not be determined.. Future work: The authors state that the current alloy design strategy could be used to develop other high-damping HEAs as well.. Quote: "Via Snoek relaxation and ordered interstitial complexes mediated strain hardening, the damping capacity of these HEAs is as high as 0.030"
